subject: The #1 mistake new trustees make (it's not what you think)
preview_text: Commingling can undo everything your trust was built for
body:
Hi there,

If there's one thing I'd drill into every new trustee, it's this: don't mix trust money with personal money.

It's called "commingling," and it's the single most common way trustees get into trouble — even when they have the best intentions.

Here's how it happens: you need to pay a trust expense, your personal checking account is right there, so you just use it. Or trust income comes in and it lands in your personal account. Seems harmless, right?

It's not.

Commingling can give a court reason to pierce your trust — meaning the legal protection you set up could be set aside. The fix is simple: separate accounts. One for trust funds, one for personal funds. Never the twain shall meet.

subject: What "piercing the trust veil" means (and how to prevent it)
preview_text: The legal concept that keeps trustees up at night — explained simply
body:
Hi there,

Yesterday I mentioned commingling. Today let's talk about why it matters so much: piercing the trust veil.

When a court "pierces" a trust, it's saying: this trust isn't really separate from the person who controls it. The legal wall between you and the trust comes down. Creditors, lawsuits, tax authorities — they can reach the trust assets directly.

Think of it like a corporation. If you run a business properly — separate accounts, proper records, regular meetings — the corporate shield holds. If you treat the business account like your personal piggy bank, a court can pierce that shield.

Trusts work the same way. The key behaviors that protect you:

- Separate bank accounts for trust and personal funds
- Documented decisions (minutes of meetings)
- Regular trust activity (distributions, investments, reviews)
- No personal use of trust assets without proper documentation

This isn't scary — it's just discipline. And it's a lot easier than most people think.

subject: Trust taxes — the simple version nobody tells you
preview_text: Understanding trust tax filings without the headache
body:
Hi there,

Trust taxes sound complicated. Let me make them simple.

A trust is its own taxpayer. It gets its own tax identification number (EIN) and files its own tax return — typically Form 1041 for a domestic trust.

Here's what most people get wrong: they think the trust's income flows onto their personal return automatically. It doesn't. The trust files separately. If the trust distributes income to beneficiaries, those distributions are reported on K-1 forms, and the beneficiaries report that income on their personal returns.

The trust itself pays tax on any income it keeps (doesn't distribute).

Three things to keep in mind:
1. File on time — the trust's tax deadline is usually April 15, same as personal returns
2. Keep trust expenses documented — many are deductible on the trust return
3. Don't file the trust return under your personal SSN — always use the trust's EIN

subject: How good trust governance saved a family (real story)
preview_text: A cautionary tale with a happy ending
body:
Hi there,

I want to share a story that shows exactly why trust governance matters.

A family I know — let's call them the Andersons — had a trust set up by their father. He passed away, and the oldest son became trustee. He meant well, but he had no system. No separate accounts. No minutes. No records of distributions. When one of the siblings asked for an accounting, he couldn't produce one.

That sibling sued. The court found that the trust had been so poorly managed — commingled funds, zero documentation, no evidence of proper trustee behavior — that the trust's protections were compromised. What should have been a clean, protected arrangement became a messy, expensive legal battle.

Now contrast that with another family. Same situation — father passes, eldest child becomes trustee. But this trustee did three things: kept separate accounts, documented every decision in writing, and held an annual review meeting (with minutes). When a creditor tried to come after the trust assets, the court looked at the records and said: this trust is clean. The shield held.

The difference wasn't the trust document. It was the behavior. The governance.

subject: HEMS — the four letters that control every distribution
preview_text: Understanding the standard that governs trust distributions
body:
Hi there,

If your trust document mentions distributions — and most do — you've probably seen the word "HEMS." It stands for Health, Education, Maintenance, and Support.

HEMS is what's called an "ascertainable standard." It gives the trustee guidance on when it's appropriate to distribute trust funds to a beneficiary. Here's what each means:

- Health: Medical care, insurance, treatments, rehab
- Education: Tuition, books, fees, reasonable living expenses while in school
- Maintenance: Keeping the beneficiary at their established standard of living
- Support: Food, shelter, clothing, transportation — the basics

The key word is "ascertainable." A court can look at a distribution and determine whether it fits within HEMS. If a trustee distributes for a reason outside HEMS — say, buying a beneficiary a sports car — that could be questioned.

This doesn't mean you need to be rigid. It means you need to document your reasoning. "I approved $5,000 for beneficiary's college tuition (Education — HEMS)" is a clean, defensible record.

Every distribution you make should have a simple written record of what, why, and how much. That's it.

subject: Your first 90 days as a trustee — a roadmap
preview_text: What to do in the first three months to set your trust up for success
body:
Hi there,

If you're newly appointed as a trustee — or if you've been one for a while but haven't really gotten organized — here's a 90-day roadmap to get your trust governance in order.

Days 1-30: Get the basics in place
- Read the entire trust document. Understand your powers and duties.
- Open a dedicated trust bank account if you don't have one.
- Get the trust's EIN and make sure tax filings are current.
- List all trust assets and their current values.
- Identify all beneficiaries and their contact information.

Days 31-60: Start documenting
- Hold your first trustee meeting (even if it's just you). Take minutes.
- Review the trust's investment strategy. Document your analysis.
- If any distributions are needed, make them and document the HEMS rationale.
- Set up a system for tracking income and expenses.

Days 61-90: Build the habit
- Schedule a recurring quarterly trustee meeting.
- Review the trust's performance against its goals.
- Prepare the trust's tax documents (Form 1041).
- Create a succession plan — who takes over if you can't?

This is exactly what TrustOffice automates. The minutes templates, the distribution tracker, the reminders, the annual review prompts — all of it. But whether you use our platform or a notebook, the important thing is that you do it.

subject: Why most trusts fail (and the simple fix)
preview_text: It's not the legal document — it's the day-to-day management
body:
Hi there,

Here's something that might surprise you: most trusts don't fail because of a drafting error. They fail because of trustee inaction.

A trust is a living thing. It needs regular attention. And when it doesn't get it, problems compound:

- No minutes = no evidence you were acting as a trustee
- No separate accounts = commingling risk
- No distributions = beneficiaries get frustrated and suspicious
- No annual review = investments drift, deadlines get missed, and the trust slowly becomes a legal fiction

The fix isn't complicated. It's just consistency. A few hours a year — maybe 4-6 total — is enough to keep a trust healthy. The problem is that without a system, those hours never happen. Life gets in the way.

subject: The annual trustee checklist (print this out)
preview_text: Everything you need to review once a year — all on one page
body:
Hi there,

Here's your annual trustee checklist. Bookmark this, print it, tape it to your desk — whatever works.

Annual Trust Review Checklist:

Banking & Accounts
[ ] Trust has its own bank account, separate from all personal accounts
[ ] No personal funds have been mixed with trust funds
[ ] All trust expenses were paid from the trust account

Documentation
[ ] Minutes exist for every trust meeting or significant decision in the past year
[ ] All distributions are documented with amount, date, beneficiary, and HEMS rationale
[ ] Trust document and any amendments are stored safely and accessible

Taxes
[ ] Trust tax return (Form 1041) has been filed or is on track to be filed
[ ] K-1 forms have been issued to beneficiaries who received distributions
[ ] Trust expenses deductible on the return have been compiled

Investments & Assets
[ ] Trust assets have been reviewed and valued in the past 12 months
[ ] Investment strategy aligns with the trust's purposes and the Prudent Investor Rule
[ ] Any changes to the investment portfolio have been documented

Beneficiaries
[ ] All beneficiaries are accounted for and contact info is current
[ ] Any beneficiary changes (births, deaths, life events) have been noted
[ ] Distribution plans for the coming year are outlined

Succession
[ ] A successor trustee is identified and knows their role
[ ] Trust documents are organized for a smooth handoff if needed

If you went through this list and found gaps, don't panic — just start fixing them. And if you want help prioritizing what to tackle first, I'm a call away:
https://trustoffice.app/book-a-call/

Best,
Jeff
